R0112.title: Office Environment Risk
R0112.definition: Office environment business security risk involves various potential threats and hazards related to business operations that may cause harm to an organization's information, systems, employees, and customer data.
R0112.description: Possible office environment business security risk scenarios include: data leakage (sensitive information, customer data, or trade secrets exposed through unauthorized access, insider leaks, or cyberattacks); cyberattacks (malware, viruses, ransomware, phishing causing business system disruption, data corruption, or theft); supply chain risk (insecure supply chains introducing malware or substandard products); social engineering (attackers obtaining sensitive employee information through impersonation or fraudulent communications); and physical security risks (unauthorized access, device loss, or insecure facility layouts).
R0112.influence: Impacts include: financial losses from data breaches, cyberattacks, and other security incidents; reputational damage reducing customer and partner trust; legal liability from data breaches; and business disruption affecting service delivery and customer satisfaction.

observables: Office access control/badge swipe records mismatch with actual on-site personnel, showing tailgating or impersonation signs
Surveillance footage in sensitive areas shows unauthorized personnel lingering for extended periods or abnormally operating equipment
Unregistered devices appear on the internal network, or sensitive data is anomalously accessed outside working hours

R0112-001.title: Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) Risk
R0112-001.definition: BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) refers to employees using their personal devices (such as phones, tablets, laptops) for work-related tasks.
R0112-001.description: BYOD presents multiple potential risk scenarios: personal devices typically lack enterprise-grade security measures and may become sources of security vulnerabilities; compliance issues may be exacerbated by difficulty monitoring personal devices; personal devices connected to the corporate network may be attacked by viruses and malware; managing and monitoring various types of personal devices is difficult; and employees who leave the company may still have access to company data.
R0112-001.influence: BYOD introduces potential harms including security vulnerabilities, data leakage, compliance issues, network security threats, device management challenges, loss of control, and post-departure access issues.

references.title: NIST SP 1800-22: Mobile Device Security: Bring Your Own Device (BYOD)

observables: A personal device connecting to the corporate network triggers anomalous data exfiltration or access to out-of-scope resources
An employee account accesses sensitive systems from an unfamiliar device/location outside working hours
Departed employees' accounts keep logging into corporate apps after their permissions were not revoked in time

R0112-002.title: Unauthorized Physical Access
R0112-002.definition: Unauthorized physical access refers to individuals or entities entering office premises, equipment areas, data centers, or other sensitive locations without explicit company or organizational approval.
R0112-002.description: This physical access may lead to information security threats involving: unauthorized personnel entering office areas through social engineering, impersonation, or other deceptive means; inadequate visitor management lacking proper registration and identity verification; unauthorized device connections by employees or visitors introducing malware; physical file and device access by unauthorized individuals; unauthorized data center access leading to illegal operations on servers and storage; and unauthorized server room access causing equipment tampering or data leakage.
R0112-002.influence: Unauthorized physical access may cause serious information security harms including theft, tampering, or destruction of confidential information; data leakage causing serious business damage; reputational loss, legal liability, and financial losses; and introduction of malware or malicious devices into the corporate network.

observables: Access control logs show the same badge appearing in different areas within a short window, or visitors entering without registration
Surveillance footage shows individuals tailgating others through access points, wearing cloned badges, or impersonating visitors
Unauthorized personnel linger in or operate equipment within server rooms/data centers outside maintenance windows

R0112-003.title: Unauthorized Device Connection
R0112-003.definition: Unauthorized device connection risk refers to unapproved or unauthorized devices (including computers, mobile devices, network equipment, etc.) connecting to the corporate network or systems, potentially causing security threats and data leakage.
R0112-003.description: Possible scenarios include: employees connecting personal devices without authorization or necessary security measures; external personnel or vendors bringing unauthorized hardware devices; unauthorized network devices (such as routers or switches) being connected and altering network topology; and attackers attempting to connect malicious devices (such as malicious USB devices or network sniffers) to execute attacks, steal information, or move laterally.
R0112-003.influence: Harms include: security threats from viruses, malware, or other threats introduced by unauthorized devices; and data leakage risk from unauthorized devices accessing, storing, or transmitting sensitive information.

observables: Internal switches detect devices with unregistered MAC addresses connecting while bypassing 802.1X authentication
An unknown USB device is plugged into an employee endpoint, followed by anomalous outbound connections or malicious processes
Rogue routers/pocket Wi-Fi hotspots appear on the office network, extending an unauthorized wireless entry point

R0112-004.title: Physical Damage and Destruction
R0112-004.definition: Physical damage and destruction risk refers to potential threats to an organization at the physical level that may cause damage or destruction to company facilities, property, or infrastructure, from factors including natural disasters, deliberate sabotage, theft, and terrorist attacks.
R0112-004.description: Possible scenarios include: natural disasters (earthquakes, fires, floods, hurricanes causing severe facility damage); deliberate sabotage (malicious destruction, arson, destructive robbery); theft and intrusion (thieves or unauthorized personnel attempting to enter facilities to steal property or cause damage); terrorist attacks; and industrial accidents (fires, explosions, or leaks damaging facilities and threatening employees and the surrounding environment).
R0112-004.influence: May lead to: financial losses from expensive repair costs and business interruption; business disruption affecting production and service delivery; reputational damage especially among the public and customers; and employee safety risks causing casualties or health issues.

observables: Critical facility zones show signs of physical intrusion, arson, or vandalism outside maintenance windows
Server room/data center environmental monitors (temperature, humidity, smoke, water leak) anomaly coupled with business system alerts
Critical equipment is manually powered off, relocated, or damaged, with suspicious individuals appearing in surveillance footage

R0112-005.title: Surveillance and Eavesdropping
R0112-005.definition: Refers to the potential for confidential information leakage, privacy violations, and other security issues in a corporate environment due to the presence of surveillance equipment or eavesdropping tools, from internal or external threats including employees, competitors, suppliers, or other malicious individuals or organizations.
R0112-005.description: Possible scenarios include: illegal eavesdropping devices installed in offices, meeting rooms, or other sensitive areas; surveillance camera abuse for monitoring employees or internal activities; electronic eavesdropping through remote access to corporate communication devices; insider employees recording confidential information using recording or photography devices; and supply chain risk where third-party suppliers are hacked and eavesdropping devices are introduced.
R0112-005.influence: Harms include: information leakage of business secrets, strategies, and other important information; privacy violations of employees or management; and reputational damage once surveillance or eavesdropping is exposed.

observables: Anomalous wireless signals or unregistered miniature transmitting devices detected in meeting rooms/office areas
Pinhole cameras, voice recorders, or other unauthorized capture devices found in sensitive areas
Enterprise communication links show anomalous traffic mirroring/diversion, suggesting man-in-the-middle eavesdropping

R0112-006.title: Wireless Network Risk
R0112-006.definition: Wireless network risk refers to potential threats and security issues when using wireless networks (Wi-Fi), which are more susceptible to various types of attacks due to their broadcast nature and wireless transmission characteristics.
R0112-006.description: Common wireless network risks include: unauthorized access (unauthorized individuals attempting to access protected wireless networks); password cracking (attackers trying to crack wireless network passwords through weak passwords, default passwords, or insecure encryption); phishing attacks (attackers setting up fake wireless networks mimicking legitimate ones to steal user information); man-in-the-middle attacks (attackers inserting themselves between users and access points to monitor or tamper with traffic); wireless interference; wireless cloning (attackers cloning legitimate access points); and wireless intrusion.
R0112-006.influence: May lead to sensitive information leakage, data tampering through man-in-the-middle attacks, unauthorized network access, and business system disruption.

observables: Rogue hotspots with SSIDs highly similar to the corporate network appear in office areas, luring employees to connect
Wireless networks show brute-force or weak-password login attempts, with a spike in authentication failure rate
After endpoints connect to unauthorized access points, traffic is hijacked or redirected by a man-in-the-middle

R0112-007.title: Wireless Access-Control Signal Replay and Cloning
R0112-007.definition: Attackers capture, copy, or replay credential signals from wireless remotes or RFID access cards to bypass physical access controls and obtain unauthorized access to facilities or equipment.
R0112-007.description:
Wireless access-control signal replay and cloning affects garage doors, campus gates, office access systems, warehouse shutters, and equipment remotes that rely on fixed codes, low-security RFID credentials, or wireless protocols without mutual authentication. An attacker can record radio signals or read credential data while a legitimate user opens a door, then clone a card, emulate the remote, or replay the original signal so that the receiver accepts an old legitimate command as a new authorization event.

Rolling codes and challenge-response mechanisms reduce direct replay risk, but implementation flaws, shared keys, overly broad synchronization windows, combined jamming and capture, relay attacks, or reader replacement can still undermine the authentication boundary. This risk concerns bypassing physical access control with wireless credentials rather than general Wi-Fi intrusion or radio interference alone.
R0112-007.influence: Attackers may bypass access controls and enter offices, data centers, warehouses, or equipment-control areas to implant devices, steal documents, cause damage, or penetrate internal networks, while weakening identity attribution in access logs.

references.title: Guidelines for Securing Radio Frequency Identification Systems - NIST SP 800-98
A Security Analysis of Garage Door Remotes and the Danger of DOR Attacks - Trend Micro Research

keywords: Wireless Access-Control Signal Replay and Cloning

observables: The same wireless credential is used at distant entrances or within an impossible time interval
Abnormal Sub-GHz recording, interference, or repeated authentication failures appear near the access-control receiver
A fixed-code remote opens a door without authorization even though the original credential was not lost
RFID events share the same credential identifier but conflict with radio characteristics, device context, or surveillance records
